title: Chapter 68 — The Blanket
paragraphs: I have given considerable attention to that not-easy subject: the skin of the whale. I have had arguments about it with experienced whalemen at sea and learned naturalists ashore. My original opinion remains unchanged, but it is only an opinion.

The question is: what and where is the skin of the whale? You already know what his blubber is. That blubber is something with the consistency of firm, close-grained beef, but tougher, more elastic and compact, and ranges from eight or ten to twelve and fifteen inches in thickness.

Now, however absurd it may seem at first to call any creature's skin that thick and dense, there are in fact no arguments against it. Because you cannot peel off any other dense covering from the whale's body but that same blubber. And the outermost layer of any animal is, by definition, its skin. True, from the unmarred surface of the sperm whale, a thin, transparent substance can be peeled off — not unlike the thinnest of tissue paper. It is almost as transparent as glass, and though very stiff and brittle when dry, is very flexible when fresh. I have several samples of it preserved, which I show to my friends. One is a piece about a foot square. I have occasionally mistaken it for the finest Italian tissue paper.

Assuming the blubber to be the skin of the whale, then when this skin — as in the case of a very large Sperm Whale — will yield the bulk of one hundred barrels of oil, and when it is considered that, by weight, that oil in its expressed state is only three-quarters, and not the entire substance of the coat — some idea may be formed of the enormous size and weight of the whale's integument.

In life, the visible surface of the Sperm Whale is not the least among the many marvels he presents. Almost without exception, it is covered with crisscrossing straight marks in dense patterns, somewhat like those in the finest Italian line engravings. But these marks do not seem to be cut into the transparent surface mentioned above. They seem to exist in the underlying substance. Nor is this strange. For just as you can see the lines on the back of your hand through a fine tissue held over it, so these marks are visible through his outer covering. In some cases, the network of these marks is so densely tangled that it resembles an old oak tree's bark. And in elderly whales, these marks grow deeper, as the wrinkles in a human face grow deeper with age.

A word or two more about this matter of the skin or blubber of the whale. It has already been said that it is stripped from him in long pieces called blanket-pieces. Like most sea terms, this one is apt and meaningful. For the whale is indeed wrapped up in his blubber as in a real blanket or bedspread — or, better yet, an Indian poncho thrown over his head and trailing below his knees. It is by reason of this cozy blanketing of his body that the whale is enabled to keep himself comfortable in all weathers, in all seas, times, and tides. What would become of a Greenland whale, say, in those shuddering, icy seas of his, if he did not carry his own furnace with him?

It does seem to me that herein we see the rare virtue of a strong individual vitality, and the rare virtue of thick walls, and the rare virtue of interior spaciousness. Admire and model yourself after the whale! Do you, too, remain warm among ice. Do you, too, live in this world without being of it. Be cool at the equator. Keep your blood fluid at the Pole.
But how easy and how hopeless to teach these fine things! Of buildings, how few are domed like St. Peter's! Of creatures, how few are vast as the whale!
